title: Fewest Flips to Alternate Bits
statement:
You get a string s made of the characters '0' and '1'. In one flip you change a single character from '0' to '1' or back.

A string alternates when no two neighbouring characters are equal, like "1010" or "010". Return the smallest number of flips that makes s alternate. Either starting character is allowed.

examples.why: Against "0101" two positions differ (indexes 2 and 3). Against "1010" all four differ. The smaller count wins.
Flip every second character to get "1010" (or "0101"). Both targets cost the same here.
"01010" needs 3 flips, while "10101" needs only 2. Starting with the existing first character is not always cheaper.

hints: There are only two alternating strings of a given length. Which are they?
Count how many positions differ from the one that starts with '0'. Can you get the other count without a second scan?
Every position matches exactly one of the two targets, so the counts add up to n. The answer is min(c, n − c).

explain.intuition:
Once the first character is chosen, the whole alternating string is fixed. So there are only two candidates: "0101…" and "1010…". The cost of reaching a target is just the number of positions where s differs from it, since each mismatch needs its own flip and no flip helps twice.

The two targets disagree at every position, so each character of s matches exactly one of them. If c positions differ from the first target, the other n − c differ from the second. Count once, take the smaller.
steps: Walk through s. At index i, the first target has '0' when i is even and '1' when it is odd.
Count the positions c where s[i] differs from that target.
pitfalls: Only trying the target that starts with s[0]. In "00100" the other start is cheaper.
Patching each equal neighbour pair from left to right. That silently keeps s[0] fixed, so it is the same mistake: on "00100" it makes 3 flips instead of 2.

solutions.title: Build both targets and compare
solutions.idea: Build the two alternating strings explicitly and count the differences against each.

solutions.title: One count, two answers
solutions.idea: Count mismatches against the target starting with '0'. The other target's count is n minus that.

followups: Instead of flipping, you may also move the first character to the end any number of times for free. How does that change the answer? (Think of a sliding window over s + s.)
The string can contain three symbols and the target cycles through them. How many targets are there now?
lcTitle: Minimum Changes To Make Alternating Binary String
